newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich says he won't betray conservatism.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich says he won't betray conservatism.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich sought to reassure Republicans Saturday that he would not betray his conservative allies while trying to seize the bipartisan high ground in the national political debate.

Speaking at a Presidents Day fundraiser attended by 1,600 of the party faithful, Gingrich said his recent overtures of bipartisanship to President Clinton and left-wing opponents such as the Rev. Jesse Jackson have stirred concern even among his closest friends.

"We Republicans need to discipline ourselves and learn some new things," said the Georgia Republican, who is struggling to repair his national image after an unprecedented House reprimand for ethics violations last month.
"I could give a partisan, biting speech here -- I think all of you know I'm capable of that. But what would it solve?" he told his audience.
"I'd feel good. You'd feel good. Every partisan could relax. And we would have set this country on a four-year path towards deadlock."

Gingrich, a staunch conservative whose confrontational style of politics once earned him the nickname of "bomb thrower," became the target of widespread criticism during a budget showdown with the White House that forced two partial shutdowns of the federal government last winter.

He soon became one of the most unpopular political figures in America. And his fortunes slumped again last December, when he admitted to violating House ethics rules following a probe of his college course, "Renewing American Civilization," which was funded with tax-exempt money.

Gingrich received a reprimand and a $300,000 penalty from the House Ethics Committee but ignored calls from his own party to step down as speaker. He still faces an investigation by the Internal Revenue Service.

After a narrowly won re-election as speaker in January, Gingrich adopted a more conciliatory tone towards Clinton and other political opponents in hopes, he said, of finding solutions to a host of social problems ranging from crime to substandard education.

"A number of my closest friends have rushed up and said, 'Are you going to be so bipartisan that you'll sell out conservatism?' or, 'When you applauded at the State of the Union, should we all be afraid?'," the 53-year-old speaker told party members who paid up to $1,000 a plate in attend Saturday's fundraiser.

"We should, all of us -- Democrat and Republican, liberal and conservative -- have the moral courage to erase the board and start over, saying, let's learn what works and let's mean it for real," he said.
"To negotiate is not to surrender. To talk is not to betray."
